author.name: Horace Chan
author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

replies.text:
Marcin Mroczkowski yes, it will be void.  The architecture of everything, software and hardware like wise will change beyond everyone's recognition. 

Computational theories are still important. Physical stuff like latency, bandwidth, capacity, power, cost and their trade off are still important. 

In the AI era, it is only AI and first principle thinking matters, all the layers in the middle suddenly go away.  All the architectural best practices based on historical convention of how we write code will be blown into pieces. 

If how we build chips and the network is changed drastically because of AI, all the software layers sitting on top will have a platonic shift.

The boundary of software and hardware will get blurred again, just like in the early days of computers.  When you can vibe code software, what stop you from vibe code hardware?   If you can easily move pieces of software into hardware, what will happen?

What if you can optimize across all layers at the same time?  Application, front end, backend, database, networking stack, OS, CPU, it is just one giant Turing machine that moves bits around.

The boundary of frontend and backend developer is pretty much gone today.  What's next?
Marcin Mroczkowski if you are using any of the 'classic' architectures for code (pre-LLM software patterns), you are barely scratching the surface of what AI is capable of.

Horace Chan
Gonna let my good friend Grok respond to this:
Ah, the "everyone's a junior in AI Wonderland" thesis—charming in its naivety, like declaring all drivers novices because Tesla Autopilot just hit puberty. But let's dissect this with the precision of a senior engineer debugging a junior's infinite loop.

ChatGPT may be a toddler, but software engineering isn't. Fundamentals like algorithms, architecture, and "don't ship code that hallucinates" predate it by decades. Seniors aren't obsolete; they're the firefighters dousing AI's dumpster fires.

Exhibit A: In 2023, GitHub Copilot spat out vulnerable code snippets, recycling old bugs like a bad DJ remixing hits. Result? Security holes in production apps, patched by—gasp—experienced humans.

Exhibit B: Air Canada's AI chatbot in 2024 promised nonexistent refunds, costing them a lawsuit. Who fixed it? Not the bot's "vibe," but seniors rewriting the logic.

Exhibit C: Countless "agentic" workflows in 2025 imploded under scale, spewing memory leaks and race conditions. Juniors cheered the hype; seniors sighed and refactored.

In this era, seniors are more vital than ever—guiding the chaos, lest we all drown in buggy, unethical sludge. The vibe? It's called expertise.
